title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: A patent portfolio tells you what a company invented yesterday; its segment revenue mix tells you who still needs it tomorrow.
epigraph.author: Industrial Underwriting Maxim

web_blocks.html: Qualcomm runs three main units: QCT (chips), QTL (licensing), and QSI (venture stakes) [1, 3]. Nonreportable units include QGOV and Data Center, which joins QCT in Q1 FY2027 [1, 3]. In FY2026 (ended September 27, 2026), GAAP revenue hit $43,120 million, down 2.6% from $44,284 million in FY2025 [1, 2]. QCT drove 86.3% of sales ($37,208 million) and $10,101 million in pre-tax profit (27.1% EBT margin) [1, 3]. QTL brought in just 12.9% of sales ($5,556 million) but earned $4,022 million in EBT (72.4% margin). That equals 28.5% of combined QCT+QTL pre-tax profit [1, 3].

web_blocks.takeaway: FY2026 shows a clear mix shift. Handsets fell 13.4% to $24.07B as Apple ramped internal modems. Meanwhile, Automotive jumped 51.7% to $6.00B ($1.99B Q4 run-rate) and IoT rose 7.8% to $7.13B, lifting non-handset QCT sales to 35.3%.

web_blocks.html: To ground these billions in physical reality, every operating stream is anchored by concrete, end-to-end commercial deployments:

Delivers on-device multimodal generative AI, console-grade ray tracing, and global 5G connectivity via 3nm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 (3rd-gen Oryon CPU + Hexagon NPU + X85/X80 modem) [22].
Sold as integrated SoC + RF front-end + PMIC chipset bundle; priced per unit via annual flagship supply contracts.

Replaces fragmented ECUs with centralized ADAS path-planning, highway hands-free driving, and cockpit compute using Snapdragon Ride Pilot and Digital Chassis SoCs [20].
Long-term Tier-1/OEM design-win contracts (5–8 year production cycles); priced per vehicle SoC/module with co-developed software stack.
Meta Platforms (Ray-Ban Meta Smart Glasses) & Windows Copilot+ OEMs (Dell, Lenovo, HP) [13, 21]
Enables ultra-low-power voice/camera multimodal AI in 50g eyewear via Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 [21], and multi-day battery life on Windows-on-ARM laptops via Snapdragon X2 Elite (45+ TOPS NPU) [13].
Sold as specialized edge SoCs and connectivity modules; priced per chip with reference-design SDKs.
Amazon Web Services (AWS) & Rack-Scale AI Customers [15, 16]
Lowers LLM inference total cost of ownership via AI200/AI250 accelerators (up to 768GB LPDDR5X per card) and 1.6T optical DSP interconnects from Alphawave Semi [15, 16].
Multi-generation hyperscale custom-silicon and optical DSP supply agreement backed by milestone warrants [16].
Grants legal freedom-to-operate across 160,000+ granted/pending patents covering 3G/4G/5G cellular SEPs and Wi-Fi/video codecs [8].
Multi-year bilateral portfolio licenses; royalty calculated as a capped percentage of wholesale device price (subject to ASP caps).
web_blocks.takeaway: Qualcomm pairs high-volume fabless chip engineering in QCT with a near-pure-margin patent toll in QTL. Multi-year auto and cloud deals now anchor that base.

web_blocks.html: A key change in FY2027 is the promotion of Data Center into its own QCT reporting stream [1, 3]. In December 2025, Qualcomm closed its $2.3 billion purchase of Alphawave IP Group plc ($1.8 billion in equity) [3, 16]. Alphawave added $235 million in post-close FY2026 sales along with high-speed SerDes and optical DSP IP [3, 16]. Qualcomm also launched AI200 (2026) and AI250 (2027) inference chips and signed a multi-generation custom-silicon and 1.6T optical deal with AWS [15, 16]. Management targets $5 billion in Data Center sales in FY2027, starting above $650 million in the December 2026 quarter [1, 5, 6].

Investors must also grasp how QCT and QTL interact when a top buyer leaves. Even when Apple replaces a Qualcomm modem chip with its in-house C2 silicon, Apple still pays Qualcomm a patent royalty under its renewed QTL license [8, 11]. That patent floor explains why QTL held a 72.4% pre-tax margin on $5,556 million of sales in FY2026 [1, 3]. Still, QTL cannot grow fast on its own. Long-term earnings growth depends on QCT scaling Automotive, IoT, and Data Center faster than Handsets shrink [1, 5].

book_paragraphs: Whenever you and I look at a technology giant with a $43 billion top line, the easiest mistake is to treat it as one homogeneous blob of "chips." At Qualcomm, nothing could be further from the truth. Under the hood, you are really looking at two fundamentally different economic engines—one that designs and ships hundreds of millions of physical silicon processors, and another that doesn't ship a single gram of sand.

The first engine is QCT, Qualcomm's semiconductor arm, which brought in $37.2 billion in fiscal 2026—about 86% of total company sales—and earned $10.1 billion before taxes, a 27.1% margin. Inside QCT, three distinct businesses are moving at very different speeds. Handsets remain the biggest piece at $24.1 billion, down 13.4% from the prior year as Apple steadily replaces Qualcomm modems with its own in-house C-series chips. Yet right alongside that contraction, Automotive surged 51.7% to $6.0 billion, crossing nearly $2 billion in the fourth quarter alone, while IoT—spanning industrial robotics, Wi-Fi 7 networking, Windows Copilot+ laptops, and smart glasses—grew nearly 8% to $7.1 billion.

To see what QCT actually sells, picture three everyday objects. In your pocket, a flagship Android phone like the Samsung Galaxy S26 runs on Qualcomm's 3-nanometer Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5—a tightly packed system-on-chip combining custom Oryon CPU cores, graphics, an AI neural processor, and a 5G modem. In your driveway, a next-generation BMW Neue Klasse electric vehicle relies on Qualcomm's Snapdragon Ride Pilot and Digital Chassis to fuse camera, radar, and cockpit displays into one software-defined nervous system. On your face, a pair of Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses uses a tiny, power-sipping Snapdragon AR1 chip so you can ask a multimodal AI assistant what you are looking at without melting the frames or draining the battery in twenty minutes.

Now contrast all of that physical engineering with the second engine: QTL, or Qualcomm Technology Licensing. In fiscal 2026, QTL generated $5.56 billion in revenue—barely 13% of the company's top line—yet it produced $4.02 billion in pre-tax earnings. That is a 72.4% pre-tax margin. QTL sells no chips. Instead, it licenses Qualcomm's massive portfolio of standard-essential 3G, 4G, and 5G patents to virtually every smartphone maker on Earth, including Apple, Samsung, Xiaomi, Huawei, and Transsion. Even when Apple stops buying a Qualcomm modem chip for an iPhone, Apple still pays Qualcomm a patent royalty under their renewed multi-year license agreement.

And just as FY2026 closed, a fourth silicon pillar stepped onto the stage. Qualcomm spent $2.3 billion to acquire Alphawave Semi in December 2025, unveiled its AI200 and AI250 rack-scale inference accelerators, and signed a multi-generation custom silicon and optical networking deal with Amazon Web Services. Starting in fiscal 2027, Data Center will break out as its own QCT revenue stream, with management targeting $5 billion in sales next year. Understanding how these four silicon pillars interact with that 72%-margin licensing vault is the key to underwriting everything that follows.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: QTL represents only 13% of Qualcomm's revenue but nearly 29% of combined QCT+QTL pre-tax profit. Any underwriting thesis must separate the durable patent-royalty floor from the more cyclical, competitive silicon growth in Automotive, IoT, and Data Center.
